docs.title: AgentIR documentation
docs.text:
Speculative execution for LLM agents. Write the agent's search and selection logic in plain Python; the runtime starts possible next steps while the decision between them is still being made, then keeps the selected one and cancels the rest.

Test-time scaling means giving an agent more compute to search for a better answer: sample several candidates, judge them, continue from the best. Every one of those judgments is a wait. While a judge model compares two answers, the next request usually sits idle, even though either answer already contains everything needed to start its continuation.

AgentIR makes that opportunity explicit. It separates the data a request needs to be built from the decision it needs to be kept. A continuation can start as soon as its data exists; the decision only determines whether its result survives. The runtime tracks both, so an agent program written without any mention of speculation still gets it, and a verification harness can prove that the answer is byte-for-byte what the serial program would have produced.

The four stages every invocation passes through. Solid edges carry data; dashed edges carry decisions. Open the diagram.

docs.text:
The manual follows the pipeline in the figure. Read the first part top to bottom once; after that, jump to whichever page you need.

How it works explains the design, one stage per page, each starting with its own diagram and ending with pointers into the source.

  1. Architecture: the whole pipeline on one page, walked through with a concrete program.
  2. Programs and handles: what you write, and the three symbolic handles that flow through it.
  3. Identity and guards: how a request gets a stable name and seed before it runs, and how a guard says whether it may be kept.
  4. The tracer: how a Python call becomes a graph node without waiting, including the hoist and loop unrolling.
  5. The scheduler: how ready work is funded, committed, squashed, retried, and recovered.
  6. Engine adapters: the three ways vLLM is driven, and the text and token wires.
  7. Tools and the tool loop: effect contracts, observation policies, and streaming tool calls.
  8. Verification: the serial reference and the two differential gates that prove speculation is invisible.

Using AgentIR is task oriented: install, run your first program, then follow the guides for control flow, tools, the built-in algorithms, models and wires, remote servers, Harbor, static compilation, timelines, and benchmarking.

Advanced covers the scheduling optimizations layered on top of the basic policy, and the experiment archive.

Reference holds the exact contracts: Python API, runtime configuration, CLI, troubleshooting, and a glossary.

docs.title: The idea in one example
docs.text:
candidates = expand(prompt, 4)                      # four samples, one prefill
scores = collect([op(grade, out_text(c), pure=True) for c in candidates])
best = choose(candidates, by=op(rank, scores, pure=True), k=1)[0]
answer = infer(cat(best, lit("\nExplain the answer:")))
return force(out_text(answer))

choose does not wait for the ranking. It returns a placeholder for "whichever candidate ranks first". When infer continues from that placeholder, the tracer registers one explanation per candidate, each carrying a condition (a guard) that says which ranking outcome would keep it. Each explanation needs only its own candidate's text to start, so the scheduler can run all four while the grader is still working. When the ranking resolves, one explanation commits and three are cancelled. force returns only the committed one.

Every request's sampling seed is derived from its logical identity, not from when it ran, so a continuation issued early produces the same tokens it would have produced after the decision. That is what lets verification demand byte identity between speculation on and off.

docs.title: Where speculation helps
docs.text:
Speculation pays off when a program exposes a continuation before the decision selecting it resolves, and the engine has spare capacity to run it. Candidate search (best-of-N, beam search, MCTS), judge-and-refine loops, and tool calls with predictable results all have that shape. Slow judges create the opportunity; a saturated GPU erases it. The benchmarking guide shows how to measure the difference honestly.

AgentIR speculates over agent decisions. That is a different level from vLLM's token-level speculative decoding, and the two compose. See scheduling optimizations before comparing them.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
This page walks one program through the whole system. It introduces every major component and the vocabulary the rest of the manual uses. Each later page in How it works zooms into one stage.

Program, trace, execute, resolve. Verification sits beside the pipeline and compares its committed output with a serial reference. Open the diagram.

docs.title: 0. The problem AgentIR solves
docs.text:
An agent that scales at test time repeats one pattern: generate candidates, evaluate them, select, continue. The evaluation is a decision, and decisions take time. A judge model reads three answers and writes a verdict; a voting function waits for the slowest sample; a critic decides whether to iterate again. During every one of these waits, the work that comes next is fully specified but cannot start, because ordinary Python needs the decision's value to know which continuation to build.

The observation behind AgentIR is that the decision is usually not a data dependency. The continuation of candidate A needs A's text. It does not need the judge's verdict to construct its prompt; it needs the verdict only to know whether its result should be kept. AgentIR calls this a weak control dependency and turns it into runtime slack: build all possible continuations, run them early, keep one.

Three requirements follow, and they shape everything in the design:

  • Soundness. A speculatively executed request must produce exactly the bytes it would produce if it ran after the decision. Otherwise speculation changes the answer.
  • Bounded cost. Speculation must never starve committed work, and losing work must be cancelled promptly.
  • Verifiability. It must be possible to prove, on a real engine, that a run with speculation and a run without produced the same committed computation.

docs.title: 1. The program
docs.text:
You write ordinary Python against a small DSL. Here is a complete program: four samples, a vote, and an explanation of the winner.

from collections import Counter
from agentir import cat, choose, collect, expand, force, infer, lit, op, out_text

def rank_by_vote(answers):
    counts = Counter(a.strip() for a in answers)
    return sorted(range(len(answers)), key=lambda i: -counts[answers[i].strip()])

def program():
    prompt = lit("Q: A pen costs 3 dollars. What do 5 pens cost? Answer with the number.\nA:")
    candidates = expand(prompt, 4, max_tokens=32)
    answers = collect([out_text(c) for c in candidates])
    ranking = op(rank_by_vote, answers, pure=True)
    selected = choose(candidates, by=ranking, k=1)[0]
    explanation = infer(cat(selected, lit("\nExplain this answer in one sentence:")), max_tokens=64)
    return force(out_text(explanation))

Nothing in the program mentions speculation. It uses three kinds of value, which are the subject of Programs and handles:

Handle What it stands for Made by Seq A token sequence: a prompt, or a prompt plus generated output. Content is never readable directly. lit, cat, infer, expand Val A future Python value on the control plane, with the world it belongs to attached. op, collect, out_text, text Choice "Whichever pool member decision d ranks r-th". A placeholder that never blocks. choose, gate

The one rule that makes the design work: selection routes by index. choose hands back positions into a pool of handles that already exist. The ranking function can compute anything it likes, but it cannot invent a new candidate. This is why every possible continuation can be constructed before the ranking is known.

docs.title: 2. The tracer
docs.text:
runtime.run(program) executes program on a tracer thread. Each DSL call does five things in microseconds and returns:

  1. Reserve a draw. A DrawId names one logical random draw by program position: lexical call site, loop path, occurrence count, lane. This happens before any guard is consulted, so identity depends only on where the call is, never on timing.
  2. Freeze the descriptor. The prompt spine (literals plus symbolic references to other nodes' outputs), model role, sampling parameters, and observation mode hash into a NodeId. The seed is derived from the NodeId.
  3. Attach the guard. The ambient guard is a conjunction of decision literals: the conditions under which this node's world exists.
  4. Register the record with the scheduler.
  5. Return a handle and keep executing user code.

The interesting case is infer(cat(selected, ...)) where selected is an unresolved Choice. The tracer performs the hoist: it registers one continuation per pool member, each guarded by the literal "decision d ranks this member first", all sharing one DrawId. This is the single mechanism that creates branch speculation, and The tracer explains it in detail together with gate, loop, and the pacing that keeps unrolling bounded. Identity and guards covers the identity ladder and the four-valued guard algebra.

docs.title: 3. The scheduler and the engines
docs.text:
The scheduler runs on one asyncio thread. For each registered record it asks two questions: is the data ready (every referenced output exists), and what is the guard's state?

Data Guard Action ready true issue as committed work, engine priority 0 ready pending issue speculatively if depth ≤ window W and speculative in-flight < budget β not ready any wait for producers any false or failed squash: abort the attempt, keep the bytes unpublished

Committed work always preempts speculative work on a full engine; the reverse never happens. Among speculative candidates the order is: demanded first, shallow before deep, structurally likely before unlikely, higher advisory hint first, then registration order. A speculative attempt that fails simply returns the record to pending; only under a true guard do engine errors become program errors. Engine death is process-wide, so it fences every request of that engine's epoch, drains them, and rebuilds once. All of this is in The scheduler.

Physical execution goes through an engine adapter with one interface: stream(prompt, params, seed, priority, request_id), abort on cancel. Three adapters exist: in-process vLLM, a judge server subprocess, and a certified remote vLLM server. Prompts travel on a wire, either strings or exact token-id tuples. Tools run on a separate tool scheduler with committed-first queues. See Engine adapters and Tools and the tool loop.

docs.title: 4. Resolving, committing, publishing
docs.text:
When an engine request finishes, its output fills the corresponding Out hole; children become data-ready even if their own guards are still pending, so speculation can chain to depth W. When the vote in the example resolves, the decision's callbacks re-evaluate every guard that mentions it: the winner's explanation commits, the other three squash, and any that are still running are aborted.

force(x) is the publication boundary. It waits for x's data and for its guard to be true, so a losing world can never leak into the return value. A false guard raises Squashed; a failed one re-raises the deciding computation's own exception. Python ops declared pure=True may run on speculative data; the default op is an effect barrier that waits for commitment, as do tools with unknown effects. Runtime.run does not return until every committed effect obligation has executed.

docs.title: 5. Verification and diagnostics
docs.text:
Every record writes a ledger row: when it was registered, became data-ready, was issued, produced its first token, finished, and had its guard resolved, plus token counts and a disposition of committed, wasted, or failed. render_timeline turns a ledger into an SVG Gantt chart.

Two differential gates establish correctness on a real engine. Gate A runs the program with speculation off and replays its recorded outputs through an independent serial reference interpreter that never hoists; the answers and the per-draw traces must agree. Gate B runs a fresh speculation-on runtime and demands that every committed node has identical bytes. agentir check runs both. Verification explains what each gate can and cannot prove.

docs.title: Experiment archive
docs.text: The scripts directory holds the drivers, analyzers, frozen protocol locks, and cluster launchers behind AgentIR's experiments. This page maps them to the question each family studies so you can find the right one. The launchers contain cluster-specific paths and resource requests; read a family's lock before adapting it.

docs.title: Agent branch speculation on math search
docs.text:
The hephaestus_beam_spec_*.sbatch launchers run beam search with a PRM judge under paired, ladder, uniform-policy, and two-GPU layouts. analyze_beam_spec_paired.py validates the artifacts and summarizes them with the paired statistics; its answer-equality gate is why bound_commit must match across arms. bench_v12_*.sh and bench_fasttts.sh describe earlier sweep profiles.

Numbers are compared relative to each system's own vLLM baseline.

docs.title: Scheduling optimizations
docs.text: The basic scheduler funds every admissible speculative record in a fixed order. Several optional lanes refine that. All but one are advisory: they change when and whether a request is funded, never what it computes, and each is bit-identical to the basic policy when its flag is off. The exception, bound commit, is an algorithmic change with a proof obligation, and it is treated separately.

docs.title: Four kinds of speculation
docs.text:
The word appears at four levels. Keep them apart when configuring or measuring.

Mechanism What runs early What verifies it Switch agent branch speculation continuations of unresolved choose, gate, loop decisions the program's own guards SpecConfig.enabled, window, max_spec_inflight tool observation prediction the next turn built on a guessed observation the observation policy's byte comparison ToolDef(obs=..., guess=...) vLLM token drafting candidate tokens inside one request the engine's token verification EngineSpec(vllm_token_drafter=...) bound commit nothing; a losing candidate stops early a monotone score bound plus k strictly better finals choose(bound=...)

docs.title: Hints
docs.text: choose(pool, by=ranking, hint=score_vals) attaches per-member evidence. A hint that resolves after the decision's records registered still lands on the decision and re-kicks the scheduler; because a speculative descendant's guard carries its ancestor's At literal, the freshest score reorders that candidate's whole subtree at any depth. Beam search passes each round's score Vals as hints, so under a window of 2 the grandchildren of the currently best candidates are funded before the children of worse ones. A wrong hint costs capacity, never correctness.

docs.title: Loser prediction
docs.text: choose(..., predict_losers=fn) registers a fast, non-blocking callable that names pool indices currently predicted not to be selected. Their pending decodes are demoted below all speculative work, and their in-flight requests are cancelled only when admissible work wants the slot. A pruned record stays admissible: a ranking that consumes its output still resolves, and a mispredicted member reissues with the same NodeId and seed, so the committed trace is byte-identical to no pruning. Beam search enables this for prm with min aggregation (--prune-margin), where a parent's previous-round aggregate is an advisory upper bound on its children.

docs.title: Expected-value gate
docs.text:
SpecConfig(ev_gate=True) replaces blind breadth with a per-record estimate:

EV(r) = P_commit(r) × T_saved(r) − C_interference(r)
  • P_commit multiplies, over the record's unresolved guard literals, a slot-world selection probability built from the decision's live member hints: a member's current rank among scored siblings, softened toward the pool prior k/P by the unscored fraction, split across its k slot worlds by a kernel around its rank, clamped to at least half a uniform share. Bound-dead members get 0.
  • T_saved sums, per decision site, an EWMA of the observed adjudication latency (from the last direct waiter's data-ready to resolution), minus the time this record has already waited. Until a site has any sample the record is cold and is gated on P alone against ev_gate_p_floor (default 0.05).
  • C_interference is the slope of an online regression of engine step interval against running batch size, times the record's max_tokens.

Speculative candidates are funded by EV descending and cut at EV ≤ 0. Demanded records are exempt for liveness. Rejected records stay pending and are re-evaluated on the next pass.

docs.title: Speculative slot preemption
docs.text: With β saturated, the basic policy freezes funding order: an early-registered candidate holds its slot even when strictly better-ordered work becomes ready behind it. SpecConfig(spec_preempt=True) lets a data-ready, admissible record blocked only by β or by slots held by other speculation cancel the worst running speculative victim it strictly dominates (shallower depth, or equal depth and strictly higher effective hint). Never demanded, committed, or nearly-done (within 25% of its budget) work. Churn is bounded: one live claim per preemptor, at most one preemption per (preemptor, victim) pair, and the victim is not re-fundable while the claim on its slot lives. The victim returns to pending with its identity intact.

docs.title: Prefix prefetch
docs.text: SpecConfig(judge_prefetch=True) warms consumers' prompt prefixes while their producer streams. When a producer has emitted prefetch_chunk_tokens new tokens, each registered consumer whose spine embeds it gets its already-materialized prefix plus the partial output sent to the consumer's engine as a max_tokens=1 request at the lowest engine priority, output discarded. Same-engine forks are skipped because decoding the parent already cached the blocks. prefetch_on_stream(source, build, model="judge") covers consumers the trace cannot express yet, such as a PRM sweep prompt that is a transformation of the candidate text: build(text_so_far) returns the prompt to warm. Prefetch traffic has no record, no ledger row, and no identity; only counters.

docs.title: Static plans
docs.text: SpecConfig(static_plan=graph.plan()) uses a compiled shape to replace the global window with per-decision depth bounds and to cap the number of distinct pool members whose subtrees are funded concurrently at k. Decisions are matched by call site. A blocked sibling stays pending and funds when a charge releases or its guard commits, so results never change.

docs.title: Depth-1 reservation
docs.text: SpecConfig(depth1_unmetered=True) exempts depth-1 continuations from β. Their count is bounded by the decision's pool, and metering them lets deeper speculation starve a late-finishing candidate's children. β keeps metering depth 2 and beyond.

docs.title: Bound commit
docs.text:
Bound commit is not speculation. It is an early-stopping rule that is part of the algorithm and is active with speculation on or off.

Suppose each candidate i has a declared upper bound b(i) on its final score that also holds for every possible truncation of its unfinished generation. Then the moment at least k rivals have resolved final scores strictly greater than b(i), candidate i provably cannot be in the top k, and its decode is terminated as done with the tokens so far, finish_reason="bound". Ties never cancel. The selection and every survivor's bytes are identical to the non-truncated algorithm on every timing schedule, because a cancelled member sits strictly below k full finals and its truncated score can only occupy ranks the selection never reads. The proof is in scheduler.bound_dead_indices, which both the scheduler and the serial reference apply verbatim.

Beam search provides the contract with bound_commit=True, valid only with scorer="prm", prm_agg="min", and a step_stop: min aggregation makes a running aggregate monotone, and a semantic step boundary keeps the parent's steps re-splitting identically inside the child's sweep, so the parent's previous-round aggregate bounds the child. selection_bounds(pool, bounds, k) opens the contest before scoring, contest.attach(i, score) adds each final as it is minted, and choose(..., bound=contest) ties it to the decision. A final that exceeds its own declared bound is counted as a contract violation. Enable the flag in both arms of any comparison, and expect truncation points to differ between runs.

docs.title: Writing rules
docs.text:
• One idea per page; one diagram per mechanism; explain a term before using it and add it to the glossary.
  • State facts in the present tense. Say what a mechanism guarantees and what it does not, in that order.
  • Every "In the code" pointer must name a real file and, where useful, a function; the checker verifies the file exists.
  • Diagrams are hand-written SVG in docs/assets/ with the palette used throughout: blue for speculative, green for committed, red for squashed, amber for decisions, dashed amber edges for guards. Give each an accessible title and description. No external renderers or fonts.
  • Never present an unexecuted GPU example as a result. Label illustrative schedules as such.
  • Frozen preregistrations in docs/benchmarks/ are excluded from the site through exclude_docs; link to them from the experiment archive rather than rewriting them.

docs.title: Changing things at the right layer
docs.text:
• A change to what a prompt is (spine, parameters, draw scoping) touches core and must keep test_ir, test_trace, test_reference, and test_compile_shape (identity parity) green.
  • A change to when work runs touches scheduler.py or tool_scheduler.py and must keep the scheduler differential green: bytes may not move.
  • A change to parsing touches tool_stream.py and the certificate; check streamed prefixes, terminal agreement, retries, and the remote protocol tests.
  • A change to a public contract updates the corresponding reference page; scripts/check_docs.py checks that every export and every SpecConfig field is documented.

Run python -m pytest (engine-free) before a real-engine agentir check.

docs.title: Your first program
docs.text: This program samples four answers, votes on them, and asks the model to explain the winner. The explanation starts before the vote finishes. It is the same program as examples/quickstart.py and needs a local GPU install.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
import re
from collections import Counter

from agentir import (
    SpecConfig, cat, choose, collect, expand, force,
    infer, lit, make_runtime, op, out_text,
)


def extract(text):
    numbers = re.findall(r"-?\d+", text or "")
    return numbers[-1] if numbers else ""


def majority(answers):
    counts = Counter(a for a in answers if a)
    return sorted(range(len(answers)), key=lambda i: -counts.get(answers[i], 0))


def program():
    q = lit(
        "Q: A pen costs 3 dollars. How much do 5 pens cost? "
        "Reason briefly, then give the number.\nA:"
    )
    traces = expand(q, 4, max_tokens=96)
    answers = collect([op(extract, out_text(t), pure=True) for t in traces])
    best = choose(traces, by=op(majority, answers, pure=True), k=1)[0]
    final = infer(cat(best, lit("\nSo, in one sentence:")), max_tokens=32)
    return force(out_text(final))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with make_runtime(
        model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct",
        spec=SpecConfig(window=2),
        engine_args={"max_model_len": 2048, "gpu_memory_utilization": 0.5},
    ) as runtime:
        print(runtime.run(program, problem_key="first"))
        rows = runtime.ledger_for("first")
        print("nodes", len(rows),
              "committed", sum(r.disposition == "committed" for r in rows),
              "issued speculatively", sum(r.speculative for r in rows))

Save it as first.py and run python first.py. It prints one sentence (the intended arithmetic is 15 dollars) and a line of ledger counts.

docs.title: What happens, line by line
docs.text:
expand(q, 4) registers four engine nodes with the same prompt and lanes 0 to 3 of one draw. They share a prefill through vLLM's prefix cache. Nothing waits: traces is a list of four Seq handles.

op(extract, out_text(t), pure=True) registers a Python task per trace that will run the moment that trace's text exists. pure=True is your promise that extract is deterministic and has no side effects; in return it may run on speculative data. collect gathers the four Vals in order.

choose(traces, by=op(majority, ...)) creates a decision whose ranking is itself a pending Val. It returns a Choice: "the trace the vote ranks first". No waiting.

infer(cat(best, ...)) is the hoist. The tracer registers four explanation nodes, one per trace, each guarded by "the vote ranks this trace first". Each needs only its own trace's text, which is a head extension (zero new prefill), so the scheduler issues them speculatively as their parents finish, while the vote is still counting.

force(out_text(final)) blocks until the vote resolves, the winning explanation has committed, and its text is on file. The three losers are squashed; if any was still decoding, its request is aborted.

docs.title: Reading the ledger line
docs.text:
issued speculatively counts engine nodes that were issued while their guard was pending. Here that is up to four explanations. If it prints 0, the vote resolved before any explanation was data-ready, which is normal for a cheap vote and a small model: there was no wait to hide. Timelines and diagnostics shows how to see this on a chart.

This example teaches the shape, not the speedup. Replace the vote with a judge model request and the overlap becomes visible.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:

  • Built-in algorithms: the same pattern in beam search, MCTS, reflexion, and others.
  • Architecture if you skipped it: what the runtime does with these calls.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: AgentIR needs Python 3.11 or newer. The package itself has no dependencies; model execution uses the pinned vLLM 0.24.0. You can trace, compile, and test programs without a GPU, and you need one (or a remote server) to run a model.

docs.title: Install the package
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/sunyxedu/AgentIR.git
cd AgentIR
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e .
agentir list

agentir list prints the built-in tasks and algorithms without loading a model. The editable install lets the CLI and examples pick up your checkout.

docs.title: Choose how models run
docs.text:
Local vLLM (GPU host)Remote vLLM (no local GPU)No model at all

vLLM publishes Linux wheels. Install the extra and run the quickstart:

python -m pip install -e '.[vllm]'
python examples/quickstart.py Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct

The first run downloads the weights and starts the engine core in a subprocess, which is why every program that creates a runtime must sit behind if __name__ == "__main__":. The quickstart uses a small context and half the GPU memory; adjust engine_args for your card.

On Apple Silicon there is no PyPI wheel. Build the vllm-metal plugin in its own virtualenv, then pip install -e /path/to/AgentIR there.

Keep the base install on the client and point it at a vLLM 0.24 server that runs AgentIR's certificate middleware:

from agentir import make_remote_runtime

runtime = make_remote_runtime(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct",
    base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
)

A generic OpenAI-compatible endpoint is not enough; the client performs a handshake against server-owned render and derender routes. Remote vLLM shows how to launch such a server.

Install the test dependencies and run the engine-free suite:

python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'
python -m pytest tests/test_ir.py tests/test_guards.py tests/test_trace.py tests/test_compile_shape.py

Static shape compilation traces a program into its graph without any engine, which is the quickest way to see what the tracer builds.

docs.text:

The documentation toolchain is separate (requirements-docs.txt); see Documentation.

docs.title: Two rules for every program
docs.text:
1. Create runtimes inside a main guard, because vLLM spawns processes.
  2. Close them. with make_runtime(...) as runtime: releases the event loop, worker pools, and engine (and reaps a judge subprocess) when the block ends.

Next: Your first program.

docs.title: Built-in algorithms
docs.text:
agentir.algos ships eight test-time-scaling algorithms written purely in the DSL. None of them mentions speculation, guards, or priorities; the runtime reads the opportunities off the graph. They are runnable baselines for agentir bench and worked examples of where weak control dependencies show up.

Each has the signature fn(question: str, **knobs) -> str and returns an extracted, normalized answer.

Algorithm Shape Where speculation appears self_consistency n chains, majority vote, explain the winner the explanation is hoisted over the vote: one fork per chain, zero new prefill best_of_n n candidates, one judge request each, pick the top judges overlap candidate generation; selection is index-only heavy n full traces, one comparative judge reads all of them, finalize the winner the finalize is hoisted over the verdict, so every candidate's finalize decodes while the judge reads cascade cheap draft, strong review, accept or escalate the escalation is infer(gate(...)): pre-decoded under the reject guard when speculation is on, conditional when off beam_search expand, score, keep the top N, repeat round t+1's children are hoisted over round t's selection, forked from every candidate sal_beam the search-and-learn PRM beam recipe, one lineage per step next-step sampling of every candidate is hoisted; a loop with a data-dependent stop reflexion draft, critique, revise until PASS rounds are traced predict-taken under continue gates; two roles give a duplex pipeline mcts UCT over a finite frontier, expand, roll out, grade, backprop expansion and rollout are hoisted over the undecided UCT pick

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
Start with heavy.py for the complete generate, judge, continue pattern in thirty lines. self_consistency.py shows control-plane ops; cascade.py shows gate; reflexion.py shows loop; mcts.py shows persistent state in Vals and a deliberate settle barrier per iteration.

common.py holds the prompts, answer extraction, score and winner parsing, and ranking helpers. These affect measured accuracy as much as the model does.

docs.title: Beam search in depth
docs.text:
beam_search.py is the most instrumented algorithm and the one the benchmark scripts target. Its knobs map to distinct mechanisms:

  • scorer: logprob (free, from the stream), judge (an LLM grader per candidate), or prm (a Math-Shepherd process reward model on the judge role, one greedy tagged token per step read through top_logprobs_of). The PRM prompt embeds a transformation of the candidate text, which is a real data dependency: the tracer waits for the text before registering the sweep.
  • step_stop: a string boundary between reasoning steps ("\n\n"), re-inserted between rounds.
  • hint=score_vals on every choose: each candidate's score re-prioritizes its whole speculative subtree the moment it resolves.
  • Boundary-extension pacing: when the window admits depth 2, the round paces after the expand, so a candidate finishing early gets its continuation issued at once.
  • prune_margin: an advisory loser predictor for prm with min aggregation (see optimizations).
  • bound_commit: bound-based early round commit, a committed algorithmic change, valid only with scorer="prm", prm_agg="min", and a step_stop (see bound commit).
  • phase_serial: a barrier between decode and grading each round, the FastTTS-style two-phase baseline.

docs.title: Keep algorithm knobs and scheduler knobs apart
docs.text:
Candidate counts, beam width, token budgets, scorer, aggregation, and bound_commit change the algorithm. Window, budget, hints, pruning, prefetch, and preemption change only when its graph runs. An A/B comparison of speculation holds the first group fixed, including bound_commit, which must be identical in both arms because it changes which dead-branch tokens exist.

CLI defaults differ from function defaults (--k is 6, best_of_n's n is 6, self_consistency's n is 8). agentir bench passes its flags through default_algo_kwargs; check that mapping in bench/runner.py when reproducing a run.

docs.title: Benchmarking
docs.text: A good benchmark answers three questions separately: did the two arms compute the same thing, which mechanism changed, and how much faster was it at the intended concurrency. agentir bench handles the mechanics; this page explains how to use it so the answer means something.

docs.title: Run the gates first
docs.text:
agentir check --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct \
  --algo beam_search --task gsm8k --offset 0 --runtime-graph check.svg

check runs both verification gates on one problem and exits non-zero on any divergence. A speedup measured on a configuration that fails the gates is not a result.

docs.title: A paired run
docs.text:
agentir bench --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct \
  --task gsm8k --algo heavy --n 20 \
  --spec both --concurrency 1 \
  --out runs/heavy.jsonl --dump-ledger runs/heavy-ledgers --runtime-graph runs/heavy-timelines

--spec both runs speculation off then on over the same problems with the same run seed and the same per-problem invocation key, so both arms sample the same tokens, then prints the paired summary: mean and percentile wall time, accuracy, answer agreement, committed and wasted tokens, speculative hit rate, and accumulated lead. The JSONL holds the metadata, arm summaries, and per-problem records.

Other modes: --spec ladder adds the serial and oracle arms (see the ablation ladder); --spec fastbase adds a phase-serial beam baseline that batches decode and grading but forbids overlap between them.

docs.title: Hold everything else fixed
docs.text:
Record, and keep identical between arms: model and revision, engine version and arguments, chat template and parser, sampling parameters, algorithm knobs, task slice, run seed, wire, and concurrency. For tools add the effect declaration, projection, predictor, and certificate. The bound-commit flag is an algorithm knob and must match in both arms, because it changes which losing-branch tokens exist.

Speculation-only knobs (--judge-prefetch, --ev-gate, --spec-preempt, --depth1-unmetered, --prune-margin) apply to the spec-on arm only, so the off arm stays a pristine baseline. vLLM token drafting is an engine setting; if you vary it, vary it explicitly in both arms rather than folding it into "spec on".

docs.title: Choose the unit
docs.text:
Question Profile Does one task finish sooner? paired per-task latency at --concurrency 1 Does a loaded server finish more tasks? a fixed higher-concurrency throughput profile, reported separately What did the speedup cost? committed versus wasted tokens, request counts, engine time Is quality preserved? paired accuracy with a declared non-inferiority margin

Warm-up, weight loading, and dataset download are separate phases; say which are timed. One task can contain dozens of overlapping requests, so per-request latency, per-task latency, and suite makespan are different numbers.

docs.title: Summarize honestly
docs.text:
agentir.bench.stats provides the paired analysis the formal scripts use: per-task aggregation in log-latency space, a cluster bootstrap over tasks for the geometric-mean speedup interval, a paired sign-flip test (exact up to 16 tasks, Monte Carlo above), Holm correction across hypotheses, and quality non-inferiority whose lower confidence bound must exceed the negative margin. The task is the statistical unit; repetitions within a task are aggregated first.

Decide the analysis before looking at the results, keep the raw records, and tie every summary to the configuration and artifact hashes that produced it. The frozen protocols in the experiment archive are examples of that discipline.

Source: bench/runner.py, bench/stats.py, bench/tasks.py.

docs.title: Static shape compilation
docs.text: agentir.compile.shape_trace runs a program once over symbolic values and returns its structure as a graph: every engine-node shell, op, decision, loop body with its back-edge, and bounded tool slot, before any model is loaded. Use it to see what the tracer will build, to serialize a program's shape, or to produce a per-decision funding plan for the scheduler.

docs.title: Compile a program
docs.text:
This runs with the base install and no GPU:

from agentir import cat, choose, collect, expand, force, infer, lit, op, out_text
from agentir.compile import shape_trace


def rank_by_length(answers):
    return sorted(range(len(answers)), key=lambda i: len(answers[i]))


def program(question):
    candidates = expand(lit(question), 3, max_tokens=64)
    answers = collect([out_text(c) for c in candidates])
    ranking = op(rank_by_length, answers, pure=True)
    best = choose(candidates, by=ranking, k=1)[0]
    final = infer(cat(best, lit("\nSummarize:")), max_tokens=32)
    return force(out_text(final))


graph = shape_trace(program, "Explain prefix caching.")
print(graph.summary())
with open("program-shape.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as output:
    output.write(graph.to_json())

The summary lists three expand shells, a collect op, a ranking op, one choose, and one guarded infer continuation. rank_by_length was never called on real text: op returns a symbol, and only a Python branch on a symbol is refused.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The shape tracer is a third context that duck-types the serial hooks: serial = True routes every primitive to it, exactly like the reference interpreter, so no new dispatch path exists in the DSL. Each primitive emits one trace event per node shell. Identity parity is structural, not re-derived: draws come from the same DrawLedger, parameters merge through the same validation, and spine templates canonicalize with the same literal merge, so a shell's precomputed identity chunks finalize to exactly the NodeId the live tracer mints once the dynamic hole digests are known.

ShapeChoice is the compiled form of the hoist: one parametric shell stands for every member's world instance, with a sel segment in its spine instead of n copies.

docs.title: Loops become loops
docs.text: The fold pass detects consecutive isomorphic blocks in the event stream (same signatures, references that shift by exactly the period, or point to the same pre-loop node) and collapses them into one body plus back-edges annotated with a trip count. A block that continues the problem literal in round 0 and a selection afterwards is absorbed as the first iteration with its literal as the init binding, so for t in range(rounds) folds to trip_count == rounds. A Python map over an array, whose references slide through pre-region values, is correctly not a loop. loop declares its structure, so the tracer emits it pre-folded with a bound trip; so does the tool loop, whose turns fold to one assistant shell plus max_calls slot shells.

docs.title: Read the graph
docs.text:
Element Meaning node shell the static part of an engine request, op, decision, or tool slot, with an identity prefix when one exists cat_data edge spine concatenation transform_data edge an opaque op control edge a selection determines whether the target survives loop body shell ids, trip count and kind, carried ports with init bindings guard pool size, k, continuations, and the maximum useful speculation depth below it

Shells whose identity binds at run time (tool slots, chat-rendered turns, dynamic-literal holes) carry an identity_note instead of a prefix. StaticGraph.from_json round-trips the JSON.

docs.title: Produce a funding plan
docs.text:
from agentir import SpecConfig

spec = SpecConfig(static_plan=graph.plan())

plan() lowers the guard structure to a StaticPlan: per decision site, a speculation-depth bound (from the longest chain of selections below it, or the global window when a loop back-edge makes it unbounded) and a sibling budget of k, since at most k of P members commit and funding more distinct members' subtrees is provably waste. The scheduler matches decisions by call site. A plan is capacity policy only: guards, identity, committed admission, and results are untouched. See static plans.

docs.title: Graph breaks
docs.text:
Any bool, len, int, str, iteration, or membership test on a symbol raises GraphBreak with the file and line of the branch. So does chat_prefix (it needs the engine's template) and the observation-decision primitives expect and classify. A graph break is a compiler boundary, not a runtime bug: the program still runs normally under the live tracer, just without a plan.

Source: compile/tracer.py, fold.py, graph.py, symbols.py; tests test_compile_shape.py, test_compile_plan.py.

docs.title: Branching and loops
docs.text: Use choose, gate, and loop whenever a decision determines which already-describable work survives. Use ordinary Python when the next request truly cannot be built without a concrete value; that is a barrier, and it is fine, just visible.

docs.title: Select and continue
docs.text:
The core pattern keeps the ranking asynchronous:

candidates = expand(prompt, 3, max_tokens=128)
scores = collect([op(score, out_text(c), pure=True) for c in candidates])
ranking = op(rank_desc, scores, pure=True)        # Val[list[int]], best first
best = choose(candidates, by=ranking, k=1)[0]
answer = infer(cat(best, lit("\nConclude in one line.")), max_tokens=64)

ranking must resolve to distinct integer positions into the pool, at least k of them, best first. A bare int is the k=1 shorthand. Scores, booleans, or repeated positions fail the decision and the failure surfaces at consumers.

Ask for k > 1 to keep several ranks. Each element is a rank-specific Choice:

top2 = choose(candidates, by=ranking, k=2)
merged = infer(cat(lit("A: "), top2[0], lit("\nB: ")))   # one Choice per cat

cat distributes over one unresolved Choice. It refuses two independent ones; force one first, or restructure around a single decision.

A hint= list of per-member Vals (the scores, say) tells the scheduler which member's continuations to fund first as evidence arrives. It cannot change the result. See optimizations.

docs.title: Keep or drop
docs.text:
keep = op(needs_detail, out_text(draft), pure=True)      # Val[bool]
more = infer(cat(gate(draft, keep), lit("\nAdd the missing detail.")))

gate(x, cond) keeps x when cond is true and has no false branch: forcing more when keep is false raises Squashed. Use it for work whose absence is fine, or inside a larger choose where the other branch provides the fallback. The cascade algorithm gates an expensive escalation on a rejection verdict so it decodes early only when speculation is on.

docs.title: Iterate until a condition says stop
docs.text:
def revise(state):
    review = infer(cat(state, lit("\nReview this answer.")), max_tokens=96)
    again = op(needs_revision, out_text(review), pure=True)   # Val[bool]
    revised = infer(cat(review, lit("\nWrite the revised answer.")), max_tokens=192)
    return revised, again

result = loop(draft, revise, max_iters=3)

body(state) returns (next_state, continue). Return the condition as a Val; do not force it to decide in Python. The tracer traces round t+1 under the assumption that round t continues, up to lookahead unresolved rounds ahead (default: the speculation window). If the condition turns out false, the extra rounds are squashed as a whole.

The returned state is the one that entered the stopping round

When round t's condition is false, loop returns states[t], the state that entered round t, not the next_state that round proposed. In the example, a review that accepts the current answer returns that answer, not a revision of it. If every condition is true through max_iters, the last next state is returned.

The reflexion algorithm is this loop with a judge-role critic; read reflexion.py for the full version.

docs.title: Hand-written round loops
docs.text: A for loop that feeds each round's selection into the next round's expand is fine, but the hoist multiplies: with every earlier selection unresolved, round t registers pool^t guarded continuations. Call pace_unrolling (from agentir.api) once per round with the selections so far; it blocks while more than lookahead of them are unresolved. If you skip it, the tracer stops you at 4096 world instances per call with an error naming the fix. Beam search in the algorithm library shows the pattern, including where in the round body to place the pace.

docs.title: What becomes a barrier
docs.text:
You write Effect Alternative force(ranking) then index the pool in Python selection is a full stop pass the Val to choose lit(force(out_text(x)) + suffix) the tracer waits for the text and loses the spine link cat(x, lit(suffix)) infer(some_val) where the Val holds a Seq waits for the value first expose the pick as a choose if handle: TypeError: a handle has no truth value gate, choose, or a deliberate force side effects inside op(..., pure=True) the purity promise is broken; the effect may run in a losing world default op, or a tool

Barriers are correct. They cost the overlap you would otherwise get, and a timeline makes them easy to spot.

docs.title: Timelines and diagnostics
docs.text: Before aggregating a benchmark, look at one problem. A timeline shows where the invocation waited, what ran early, and what survived; a wall-clock number alone cannot tell you whether the overlap you expected happened.

docs.title: Render a timeline
docs.text:
from agentir import render_timeline
from agentir.diagnostics.viz import TimelinePanel

rows = runtime.ledger_for("first")
events = runtime.events_for("first")
render_timeline(TimelinePanel("spec on, W=2", rows, events), "first.svg", title="first program")

The SVG is written by hand, with no plotting dependency. Pass a list of panels to stack runs on one time axis; agentir check --runtime-graph does exactly that for the spec-off and spec-on arms, and agentir bench --runtime-graph DIR writes one file per problem and arm. --dump-ledger DIR saves the raw rows as JSONL.

docs.title: Read the chart
docs.text:
Each engine node is a lane. A diamond marks registration; a thin gray line is the queue between data-ready and issue; the bar runs from issue to done, with a lighter head for prefill and a shaded body for decode.

Color Meaning blue issued while the guard was pending (speculative) green committed; a blue bar turns green at guard resolution red wasted or failed: finished or aborted in a losing world amber band control-plane ops, packed into lanes dashed red vertical a decision resolved

Registered-but-never-issued nodes appear as markers only, with "squashed before issue" when their guard turned false first. The header of each panel summarizes wall time, committed and squashed counts, speculative hit rate, accumulated lead, and committed versus wasted tokens.

docs.title: The ledger fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning A long gap before it means t_reg the tracer registered the node the program had not reached this call yet t_data_ready every referenced output existed an upstream generation, op, or tool was still running t_issue a physical attempt started no free slot, budget exhausted, or lower funding priority t_first first stream event prefill and engine queueing; equals t_done for final-granularity attempts t_done the stream ended decode time t_guard_resolved the keep-or-cancel decision landed selection latency

speculative says how the node was issued; disposition says what happened to its work. Both matter: a node can be issued speculatively and commit, or finish committed-priority and still be wasted later. cached_tokens is the engine's own prefix-cache count; -1 means the engine did not report it. fork_parent marks nodes whose prompt extends a parent's full state, which is what makes a cache hit possible, not proof of one.

docs.title: Diagnose a disappointing run
docs.text:
What you see Look at no blue bars did the decision resolve before its children were data-ready? A cheap vote hides nothing. Check window and max_spec_inflight long gray queues on green bars the engine is full; committed work is waiting behind other committed work, or max_inflight is low mostly red wide pools with poor selection accuracy, or a deep window over an unlikely branch large lead sum, small wall gain leads overlap in time, or something else is on the critical path (a PRM sweep waiting for text, a render round trip) correct predictions, no gain the tool is fast, the predictor is slow, or remote publishes calls only at turn end

The lead metric sums t_guard_resolved − t_issue over committed speculative nodes. Several nodes accumulate lead over the same interval, so it is an upper bound on saved time, never an elapsed-time figure.

docs.title: Beyond the ledger
docs.text:
runtime.snapshot() returns scheduler counters (pending, in flight, spec in flight, engine recovery state) and tool-scheduler queue depths. runtime.counters holds named event counts: preempted, pruned, spec_retries, prefetch_issued, engine_deaths, and others. bench.gpu_telemetry and bench.vllm_metrics_telemetry sample nvidia-smi and vLLM's Prometheus endpoint into JSONL for experiments; their idle-time statistics are proxies and are named as such.

Continue with benchmarking to turn one trace into a controlled comparison.

docs.title: Harbor and Terminal-Bench
docs.text: AgentIR ships a Harbor 0.16.1 agent, agentir.integrations.harbor.agent:AgentIRHarborAgent. Harbor owns the task container and trial lifecycle; AgentIR owns the model program, which is infer(instruction, tools={"shell": ...}) with the container's shell as the one tool.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Harbor needs Python 3.12 or newer. From the AgentIR checkout:

uv venv --python 3.12 .venv-harbor
source .venv-harbor/bin/activate
uv pip install -e '.[harbor]'

Start a certified vLLM server for the model you want to evaluate.

docs.title: Run a trial
docs.text:
harbor run \
  --dataset terminal-bench@2.0 \
  --agent agentir.integrations.harbor.agent:AgentIRHarborAgent \
  --model openai/Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct \
  --agent-kwarg model_endpoint=http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 \
  --agent-kwarg runner_backend=remote_vllm_tier1 \
  --agent-kwarg spec_enabled=false \
  --agent-kwarg max_turns=32 \
  --agent-kwarg shell_timeout_sec=120 \
  --n-concurrent 1

spec_enabled=true is the speculation-on arm; it sets SpecConfig.enabled for real, not just a label. runner_backend=in_process_vllm loads the model in the Harbor process instead (install the vllm extra there); there is no fallback between the two backends.

docs.title: How the shell tool crosses the boundary
docs.text:
Harbor's environment is asynchronous and owns the event loop. The synchronous AgentIR program runs in a worker thread; every shell call is posted back to Harbor's loop with run_coroutine_threadsafe, and trial cancellation propagates to in-flight commands.

The shell ToolDef has effect="unknown": no speculative branch ever runs a command. Its observation policy renders one canonical JSON image with stdout, stderr, return code, timeout flag, error, and truncation metadata (each stream capped at 65,536 characters, head and tail preserved). Its predictor guesses the common silent-success image, so the model's next turn can be decoded while a committed command is still running; exact comparison decides whether that turn survives. A malformed call is reported back to the model as an observation rather than aborting the trial.

docs.title: What gets recorded
docs.text: The adapter writes an ATIF v1.7 trajectory after every observation, so a timeout still leaves an auditable record. Each shell step keeps the raw provider result, timing, and effective timeout. The final step carries token counts from the ledger, the effective backend and endpoint, the certificate digest, and the full runtime configuration. Warmed runtimes are cached per exact configuration and arm, reference-counted, and fork-aware; close_cached_runtimes() releases them.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
All runner settings are AGENTIR_HARBOR_* environment variables, read once per process:

Variable Default Meaning BACKEND remote_vllm_tier1 default backend; runner_backend overrides per trial TIER1_ENDPOINT trial endpoint explicit server base URL TIER1_API_KEY unset bearer token TIER1_EXPECTED_VERSION 0.24.0 server version pin; empty disables the pin, not the certificate TIER1_EXPECTED_CERTIFICATE_SHA256 unset exact deployment pin MAX_INFLIGHT 32 engine request cap MAX_TOKENS 1024 per-turn budget MAX_CALLS 8 pre-reserved call slots per turn TEMPERATURE 0 plus optional TOP_P, TOP_K, MIN_P, PRESENCE_PENALTY, REPETITION_PENALTY INFERENCE_TIMEOUT_SEC 1800 tool-loop, decision, and drain timeout BRIDGE_GRACE_SEC 15 extra time for the shell bridge to cancel OUTPUT_CHAR_LIMIT 65536 per-stream image cap SPEC_WINDOW, MAX_SPEC_INFLIGHT 2, 8 speculation window and budget RUN_SEED 20260708 runtime seed ENGINE_ARGS, DEVICES {}, unset in-process backend only THINKING_TOKEN_BUDGET, CHAT_TEMPLATE_KWARGS unset, {} server render controls SYSTEM_PROMPT built in the terminal-agent system prompt

runner.py validates every value; the effective configuration is archived in the trajectory.

docs.title: A custom runner
docs.text:
Set runner_import_path=module:callable to replace the model side while keeping Harbor's environment and trajectory handling. The contract is an async callable (RunnerRequest, execute_shell) -> RunnerResult, where execute_shell(ShellRequest) -> ShellObservation and optionally exposes .reject(arguments, error) for calls the runner refuses to execute. The types live in agentir.integrations.harbor.protocol and have no Harbor dependency, so a runner can be tested without Harbor installed.

Formal Terminal-Bench experiments use locked launchers and analyzers; see the experiment archive.

docs.title: Models, roles, and wires
docs.text: This page covers the local runtime: creating it, giving models roles, choosing a wire, rendering chat prompts, and freezing generation settings. The mechanics are in Engine adapters.

docs.title: Create a runtime
docs.text:
from agentir import SpecConfig, make_runtime

runtime = make_runtime(
    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct",
    max_inflight=32,
    engine_args={"max_model_len": 2048, "gpu_memory_utilization": 0.5},
    spec=SpecConfig(window=2, max_spec_inflight=8),
)

Weights load on first use or on runtime.warm(). engine_args forwards to vLLM's AsyncEngineArgs. max_inflight caps AgentIR requests per engine and is also passed as max_num_seqs, so the engine is sized to exactly what the scheduler will send. Prefix caching and priority scheduling are required and enabled by default; the engine refuses a configuration that turns them off.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Programs say model="main" or model="judge", never a model id. make_runtime creates main and aliases judge to it. Give the judge its own engine with any of:

make_runtime(model=M, judge_model=PRM)                     # second model, same GPU
make_runtime(model=M, judge_devices="1")                   # same model, its own GPU
make_runtime(model=M, judge_model=PRM, judge_process=True) # subprocess server, own GIL
make_runtime(model=M, judge_model=PRM, judge_server_attach="http://127.0.0.1:8100")

judge_process is worth it when two small engines in one interpreter serialize on the GIL; it is text-wire only and serves the one-token scoring workload. For more roles, build Runtime(models={role: ModelSpec(role, EngineSpec(...))}, role_aliases=...) directly. Engines are deduplicated by their full resolved configuration, so two roles with identical specs share one physical engine.

docs.title: Wires
docs.text:
wire= Atoms Pick it for "text" (default) strings completion-style prompts, judge-server scoring "tokens" exact token-id tuples tool loops, chat and thinking models whose boundary tokens must round-trip exactly

On the token wire, continuations are exact token prefixes and the tokenizer is the engine's own. Several engines may share a token wire only if their tokenizer programs are byte-identical; the runtime checks this at warm-up and refuses otherwise.

docs.title: Chat prompts
docs.text:
Chat and thinking models need their template. Render it through the role's engine and pass the result to lit:

prefix = runtime.chat_prefix(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain why the sky is blue."}],
    role="main",
)

def program():
    return force(out_text(infer(lit(prefix), max_tokens=128)))

chat_prefix returns a string on the text wire and a token tuple on the token wire (Harmony models always render to tokens). Pass tools= to render function schemas into the system turn. chat_template_kwargs on the runtime (and judge_chat_template_kwargs, which inherits from it unless set) is canonical, identity-bearing configuration. The built-in algorithms take chat=True to render their prompts this way.

docs.title: Generation settings
docs.text:
Sampling parameters are validated and frozen into the node identity at trace time. Runtime defaults are max_tokens=512, temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95, overridable with default_params=. The accepted keys are listed in runtime configuration; anything else is an error rather than a silently dropped field. There is no per-call seed: it is derived from identity.

structured= takes exactly one of json, regex, choice, grammar, json_object, structural_tag. In tool loops, structural tags are compiled in a preflight before the turn is admitted, so a grammar the engine rejects fails at trace time rather than mid-speculation.

docs.title: Two speculations, two switches
docs.text: SpecConfig.enabled controls AgentIR's branch speculation. vLLM's token drafting is an engine setting (EngineSpec(vllm_token_drafter={...}), or speculative_config in engine_args). They are independent and identity-bearing in different places: the drafter is part of the engine key, branch speculation is not part of any identity at all. A drafting engine rejects min_p and logit_bias by key presence. See four kinds of speculation.

docs.title: Event granularity
docs.text: event_granularity="auto" lets a committed request with no incremental consumer take one terminal stream event instead of one per engine step, which removes per-step host work on the loop thread. Speculative requests, streamed tool parsers, prefetch sources, and bound-commit targets keep the delta wire. Bytes are identical either way; only ledger t_first loses its first-token meaning for final-granularity attempts.

docs.title: Remote vLLM
docs.text: make_remote_runtime runs the tracer and scheduler on the client and delegates tokenization, chat rendering, generation, and tool parsing to a certified vLLM 0.24 server. The client needs neither vLLM nor a tokenizer. The protocol is AgentIR's own token-in/token-out contract, not the OpenAI chat API, so the server must run AgentIR's middleware.

docs.title: Launch the server
docs.text:
Install the same AgentIR checkout into the server's vLLM environment so the middleware is importable, then:

python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
  --model Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml \
  --middleware agentir.execution.vllm_certificate.middleware \
  --scheduling-policy priority \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --generation-config vllm

The tool parser must match the model family (the middleware only certifies audited parser pairs: hermes+qwen3, qwen3_xml, qwen3_coder+qwen3). Check the certificate route once the server is up:

curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/agentir/tier1/certificate

A 503 here means the server state could not be certified; read the message rather than working around it.

docs.title: Connect the client
docs.text:
from agentir import force, infer, lit, make_remote_runtime, out_text


def program():
    return force(out_text(infer(lit("The capital of France is"), max_tokens=32)))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with make_remote_runtime(
        model="Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct",
        base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
    ) as runtime:
        print(runtime.run(program))

The remote runtime is always on the token wire and exposes main with judge aliased to it. Pass api_key= or headers= when the server requires them; a trailing /v1 on the URL is normalized away.

docs.title: What one request does
docs.text:
Step Route Client-side guarantee handshake GET /v1/agentir/tier1/certificate version pin, served model, parser names, and certificate digest are checked; the instance id is remembered render POST /v1/agentir/tier1/render exact prompt token ids and the server's complete SamplingParams are frozen into the E-node's identity as a _remote_tier1 envelope generate POST /inference/v1/generate token in, token out, buffered SSE; cancellation closes the socket, which is vLLM's abort derender POST /v1/agentir/tier1/derender the server re-renders the original request, checks digests, and runs its completed-output parser tokenize /tokenize, /detokenize the token wire's encode and decode

Every protected request carries the certificate digest and instance id as headers. A mismatch (412 or 428) is treated as engine death: the client fences everything issued against that instance, re-handshakes once, and either continues or poisons the engine's records with the cause. expected_certificate_sha256= pins a deployment exactly for a controlled experiment.

docs.title: The streaming boundary
docs.text:
Remote mode publishes tool calls after generation and derendering finish. It does not deliver the in-process adapter's mid-decode call events, because the parser lives on the server and only runs on completed output. A predicted next turn can still overlap the real tool execution once the call is known, so the second overlap of the tool loop is kept and the first is not. Keep this in mind when comparing local and remote latencies.

Structural-tag constraints cannot be preflighted remotely, so the client refuses them rather than risk admitting a request the server's grammar compiler will reject.

docs.title: Caching and connections
docs.text:
Successful renders are memoized in a single-flight LRU (render_cache_entries, default 128) keyed by certificate, instance, and canonical request. Ordinary JSON calls reuse pooled HTTP/1.1 connections; SSE connections are discarded after [DONE]. A restart or instance change clears the memo and the pool.

The server side is documented in vllm_certificate.py; the client in remote.py. Both are exercised without a GPU by tests/test_remote_tier1.py and tests/test_vllm_certificate.py.

docs.title: Defining tools
docs.text: A tool adds two contracts to a program: when its body may run and what the model gets to see of its result. Declare both. A result that is easy to predict says nothing about whether the side effect is safe to repeat.

docs.title: A tool the model can call
docs.text:
from agentir import Exact, ToolDef, force, infer, make_runtime, out_text

CAPITALS = {"France": "Paris", "Japan": "Tokyo"}


def lookup_capital(args):                 # one dict argument, not kwargs
    return CAPITALS.get(args["country"], "Unknown")


def program():
    reply = infer(
        "Use the lookup tool to find the capital of France.",
        tools={
            "lookup_capital": ToolDef(
                lookup_capital,
                effect="speculable",
                obs=Exact(),
                description="Look up a country's capital.",
                input_schema={
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {"country": {"type": "string"}},
                    "required": ["country"],
                    "additionalProperties": False,
                },
            ),
        },
        max_turns=4,
        max_tokens=128,
    )
    return force(out_text(reply))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with make_runtime(model="Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct", wire="tokens") as runtime:
        print(runtime.run(program))

infer(task, tools=...) runs the autonomous loop: render the conversation with the model's chat template, stream the assistant turn through vLLM's parser for that model family, execute the calls, feed back observations, repeat for up to max_turns. It returns the final assistant turn as a Seq. The loop requires wire="tokens" and a model from a supported family. input_schema is the JSON Schema of the argument object; AgentIR adds the provider's function wrapper.

docs.title: Choose the effect class
docs.text:
effect Body runs Promise you make "unknown" (default) only after the turn that called it has committed; once; no retries none "speculable" as soon as the tool scheduler admits it, possibly for a branch that later loses; up to three tries per phase re-running and discarding is harmless

An in-memory lookup is speculable. A shell command, a payment, a file write, or a query against changing data is unknown unless you have decided otherwise. The Harbor shell tool is unknown. Remember that a Python body which has started cannot be stopped; cancellation only prevents an unstarted body from being delivered.

docs.title: Choose what the model observes
docs.text:
The policy maps the raw return value to an image (a string, or JSON rendered canonically), and declares which candidate images may stand in for it before the tool finishes.

Policy Image When Exact() the projected result; guesses must match byte for byte the full result matters Ignore(text="done") a constant; never reads the result only completion matters Project(alpha) alpha(raw) the model needs a stable subset (a status code, a summary field) Enum(cases, by=key_fn) one of the declared representatives, or the real result through a hole() case the outcome space is finite and part of the tool's interface

Ignore and Project change what the agent knows. They are semantic choices, not shortcuts.

docs.title: Add a prediction
docs.text:
ToolDef(lookup_capital, effect="speculable", obs=Exact(), guess="Paris")

While the tool runs, the next assistant turn is decoded against "Paris". When the real image arrives the loop compares bytes: a hit keeps that turn, a miss squashes it and decodes the turn against the real image. With an unknown-effect tool the body still waits for commitment, but the predicted next turn can overlap it once the calling turn is committed.

A guess can also be a callable (state, call) -> str | Val | Seq, including one that traces DSL calls to a draft model. Predictor code runs in an advisory scope: model requests and speculable tools are allowed, unknown effects are not. A predictor that is still running when the real observation lands is abandoned.

The default predictor

ToolDef(fn) with neither obs nor guess gets Exact() plus a default draft predictor (a 32-token same-role sample, two candidates at first, calibrated online). Passing obs=Exact() explicitly, or guess=None, turns the predictor off. Keep this in mind when reading request counts in a benchmark.

docs.title: Tools placed directly in the graph
docs.text:
When the program, not the model, decides to call a tool:

from agentir import cat, expect, force, infer, lit, obs, observe, tool, out_text

def program():
    t = tool(lookup_capital, {"country": "France"}, name="lookup_capital", effect="speculable")
    guessed = expect(t, "Paris")                        # Choice: hit branch or real-image branch
    reply = infer(cat(lit("The lookup returned: "), guessed), max_tokens=48)
    return force(out_text(reply))
  • obs(t) splices the image into a prompt as a late-binding segment.
  • observe(t) returns the structured image as a Val for Python code.
  • ack(t) resolves when the body finished, without reading anything.
  • expect(t, guess) is a hit-or-miss decision; classify(t, cases) routes an exact image through a closed mapping and treats anything else as an error.
  • after= orders one tool behind other tools or ops without consuming their values or failures.

Arguments may contain Val and Choice handles anywhere in the JSON tree; they resolve before the tool identity is hashed. A Seq is rejected: read it out with an exit first.

docs.title: Bounds
docs.text:
max_turns bounds assistant rounds. max_calls (default 8) bounds the number of call slots the loop pre-reserves per turn for early dispatch; more calls than that are still executed, at a barrier. Neither is a safety limit on external actions; put that in the tool body.

The mechanics behind all of this, including the streaming parser and the round template, are in Tools and the tool loop.

docs.title: Engine adapters
docs.text: The scheduler never touches vLLM directly. It talks to an engine adapter with one method, stream(...), plus warm, tokenizer, restart, and shutdown. Three adapters implement that interface. This page explains what the scheduler needs from an engine, how each adapter provides it, and how prompts are represented on the way in and out.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
async for event in engine.stream(
    prompt=atoms,            # str on the text wire, list[int] on the token wire
    params=frozen_params,    # the validated, identity-bearing sampling parameters
    seed=record.seed,        # derived from the NodeId
    priority=depth_or_zero,  # 0 for committed work, guard depth for speculation
    request_id=attempt.id,   # fresh per attempt, never reused
    want_logprobs=..., want_token_ids=..., event_granularity="delta" | "final",
):
    ...

Cancelling the consuming task must abort the request in the engine. Every event is a StreamEvent with text, token ids, logprobs, top-k alternatives, finish and stop reasons, prompt and cached token counts. Consumers aggregate events, so a "final" delivery (one terminal event) and a "delta" delivery (one event per engine step) commit identical bytes; granularity changes host overhead, never semantics.

Each scheduler action maps onto one engine call:

Scheduler action Engine call committed or speculative issue generate(prompt, SamplingParams(seed=...), request_id, priority=0 or depth) squash or preempt cancel the task; the generator's cleanup aborts the request exactly once fork of a parent's output nothing special: vLLM's prefix cache reuses the parent's KV blocks, and num_cached_tokens reports it logprob scoring SamplingParams(logprobs=k)

vLLM's priority queue serves smaller values first, which is why committed work is 0 and speculation is its positive depth. Sibling draws of an expand are separate requests on purpose: vLLM's n>1 derives child seeds arithmetically from the parent's, and AgentIR sibling seeds are independent digests.

docs.title: Wires: what an atom is
docs.text:
The IR is generic over atoms. Two wires exist, chosen per runtime with wire="text" or wire="tokens".

Wire Atoms Prompt reaches the engine as Use when text (default) str a string the engine tokenizes plain completion programs; judge-server scoring tokens tuple[int, ...] a TokensPrompt id array tool loops and chat boundaries that must survive without a decode/re-encode round trip

On the token wire a continuation is an exact token-level prefix of its parent, so the cache hit is exact; on the text wire it degrades only at block boundaries. The tokenizer comes from the engine itself. With several engines on a token wire, the runtime certifies at warm-up that their tokenizer programs are byte-identical (a fingerprint of the fast tokenizer's backend JSON plus special-token ids), not merely the same vocabulary size.

The exact stream text is kept as a sidecar alongside token ids: vLLM may return special or stop tokens while omitting them from the text, and out_text must return what the engine actually said.

docs.title: In-process vLLM
docs.text:
VLLMEngine owns an AsyncLLMEngine built with prefix caching and priority scheduling. Weights load on first use, once, on the loop thread. Device pinning sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES only during that construction window, so two engines can live on different GPUs in one process.

The first thing the adapter does after construction is a capability handshake. It records the vLLM version, resolved engine args, parser configuration, and drafter settings, and fails fast on missing correctness-critical capabilities: generate and abort must exist, RequestOutputKind.DELTA must exist, and the version must match the pinned expected_version (0.24.0 by default), because version drift invalidates any byte-equality certification. Optional capabilities missing (such as FINAL_ONLY delivery) only disable the corresponding optimization.

The engine key that deduplicates physical engines digests the whole resolved configuration: model, devices, reasoning parser, token drafter, and every engine argument. Two EngineSpecs with the same model but different memory limits are two engines.

docs.title: Judge server subprocess
docs.text:
Two in-process engines share one Python interpreter, so at small model scale their host loops serialize on the GIL: one engine's sampler and detokenizer sit between the other's decode steps. make_runtime(judge_process=True) instead launches the judge role as a vllm serve-style subprocess with its own GIL and CUDA context, speaking the OpenAI /v1/completions endpoint. That is all a process-reward sweep needs: one greedy token per step whose top-k alternatives arrive as top_logprobs.

Readiness is fail-closed: health, served-model identity, version pin, and a contract probe that requests one token with full top-k and checks the response shape. The subprocess is reaped synchronously in Runtime.close so the next benchmark arm never races a dying server for GPU memory. This mode is text-wire only.

docs.title: Certified remote vLLM
docs.text:
make_remote_runtime keeps the tracer and scheduler on the client and moves everything model-specific to a vLLM 0.24 server: tokenization, chat rendering, generation, and tool-call parsing. The client needs no vLLM and no tokenizer; it uses only the standard library.

The protocol is three server-owned routes plus the native token-in/token-out generate route:

Step Route What it does handshake GET /v1/agentir/tier1/certificate Returns a canonical JSON certificate of the model revision, tokenizer, chat template, parser classes, and structured-output settings, with a digest header and an instance id render POST /v1/agentir/tier1/render Turns messages plus tool schemas into exact prompt token ids and the server's complete SamplingParams, after the parser's adjust_request generate POST /inference/v1/generate Token-in, token-out streaming derender POST /v1/agentir/tier1/derender Re-renders the original request, checks digests, and runs the completed-output parser

Every protected request carries the certificate digest and instance id as headers; the server answers 412 or 428 if they do not match, and the client treats that as engine death and re-handshakes. The render result is frozen into the E-node's parameters as a _remote_tier1 envelope, so the server's exact sampling identity is part of the NodeId. Successful renders are memoized in a small single-flight LRU keyed by certificate, instance, and canonical request.

The server side is agentir.execution.vllm_certificate.middleware, loaded with vllm serve --middleware .... It builds the certificate only from vLLM's resolved application state and refuses to serve if the parser combination is outside the audited set.

Remote mode is terminal-only: tool calls are published after generation and derendering finish, not mid-decode. Tools and the tool loop explains what that costs.

docs.title: Model roles
docs.text:
Programs name roles, not models: infer(x, model="judge"). A Runtime maps roles to ModelSpecs, each binding an engine spec and canonical chat-template arguments. make_runtime creates main and aliases judge to it unless you pass judge_model or judge_devices. The same beam-search program therefore runs single-engine or with a dedicated verifier engine depending only on configuration.

Runtime.chat_prefix(messages, role=..., tools=...) renders through the role's own template and tokenizer (or the remote render route), returning a string or token tuple to pass to lit. Harmony models (GPT-OSS) render through vLLM's Harmony stack and require the token wire.
